The amount of interest you can earn from a savings account depends on the annual percentage rate (APY). This is a measure of your total earnings after one year when considering the base interest rate and how often interest compounds (savings account interest typically compounds daily).

Say you put $1,000 in a savings account at the average interest rate of 0.38% with daily compounding. At the end of one year, your balance would grow to $1,003.81 — your initial $1,000 deposit, plus just $3.81 in interest.
Now, let's say you choose a high-yield savings account that offers 4% APY instead. In this case, your balance would grow to $1,040.81 over the same period, which includes $40.81 in interest.

The more you deposit in an HYSA, the more you stand to earn. If we took our same example of a high-yield savings account at 4% APY, but deposited $10,000, your total balance after one year would be $10,408.08, meaning you'd earn $408.08 in interest. ​​

Deposit account rates — including savings rates — are tied to the federal funds rate . This is the target interest rate set by the Federal Reserve; when it increases its target rate, deposit account rates usually increase. Conversely, when the Fed lowers its rate, deposit rates fall.

Savings account interest rates have fluctuated quite a bit over the past couple of decades. From 2010 to about 2015, rates were rock-bottom, hovering between 0.06% and 0.10%. This was largely due to the 2008 financial crisis​ and the Federal Reserve 's decision to lower its target rate to near zero in order to spur economic growth.

From 2015 to 2018, interest rates gradually increased. However, they remained low by historical standards. Then, the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 led to another sharp decrease in rates as the Fed cut rates again to stimulate the economy. This brought average savings interest rates down to new lows, around 0.05% to 0.06%, by mid-2021.

Since then, savings account rates have recovered considerably, largely driven by the Fed's interest rate hikes in response to skyrocketing inflation. However, the Fed finally lowered the federal funds rate toward the end of 2024 and continued to do so throughout 2025. As a result, deposit rates have steadily declined. So far in 2026, the Fed has kept rates unchanged
Is now a good time to put your money in a high-yield savings account?

Choosing where to put your money is an important decision, and there are a few factors you should consider when evaluating your options. A high-yield savings account could make sense if you're looking for a secure place to hold shorter-term savings while earning a solid return.

Interest rates: One of the most important features of a savings account is the interest rate. It's important to shop around and compare the best offers to ensure your money will grow over time. Considering that savings rates will likely drop in the near future, opening a high-yield savings account now will allow you to take advantage of historically high rates.

Goals: Today's high-yield savings accounts offer rates we haven't seen in more than a decade. That said, savings rates still don't match average returns for the stock market. If you're saving for a long-term goal like retirement, a savings account probably isn't the best place to put your money, since your balance won't grow at a pace that will allow you to reach your target. However, if you're saving for a financial emergency, a down payment on a home or car, holiday gifts, or another short-term goal, a savings account is a great place to hold those funds.

Accessibility: Certain types of accounts and investments may provide higher returns than a savings account, but may make it difficult to access your funds in a pinch. For example, if you put your savings in a certificate of deposit (CD) and need to access the money before the maturity date, you could be subject to an early withdrawal penalty. So, if you want to be able to dip into your savings as needed, a high-yield savings account is likely the better choice.
Security: In most cases, savings accounts are insured by the FDIC up to the federal limit. They also can't lose money due to fluctuations in the market, making them a low-risk option.
Do online banks have the best savings account rates?

Online banks operate exclusively via the web. This significantly reduces their overhead costs, so they're able to pass those savings onto customers in the form of high deposit rates and low fees. In fact, many of the best high-yield savings accounts also come with zero monthly fees or minimum opening deposit requirements. If you're searching for the best savings interest rates, online banks are a great place to start .

That said, online banks aren't the only place you can find savings accounts with rates that range between 3% and 4% APY. Credit unions are not-for-profit financial cooperatives known for offering competitive rates and fewer fees. Many credit unions have requirements that must be met to become a member, though some allow just about anyone to join.
How to open a high-yield savings account
The requirements involved in opening a savings account vary by financial institution. However, if you're ready to open an account, you can follow these general steps:

Research savings account rates: Of course, when choosing a savings account, one of the most important factors to evaluate is the interest rate. Be sure that you select a savings account with a competitive rate to help your money grow.

Figure out your must-haves: Although savings account interest rates should be top of mind, that's not the only factor to consider. You'll also want to think about what else you need from your account, whether it's no minimum-balance requirement , low fees, or other perks. Finding a savings account with a solid rate that also helps you achieve your goals is key.

Prepare documentation: Opening a bank account requires you to provide a few important personal details and documents. Before you start your application, be sure you have your Social Security number, driver's license or passport number, and proof of address.

Fill out the application: In many cases, you can apply for a savings account online. However, some financial institutions may require you to visit the branch in person to apply. Either way, the application for a new savings account should only take a few minutes to complete. In many cases, you'll get your approval decision instantly.

Fund your account: Once your savings account application is approved, you'll need to add funds to the account. Be sure you're aware of any minimum opening deposit requirements and the timeline for funding.
Is a high-yield savings account right for you?

A high-yield savings account is a good fit if you want to earn a competitive return on money you'll need in the near future while keeping it safe and accessible. It's important to not only consider whether the interest rate is attractive, but whether the account matches the purpose of your savings.
You want to maximize your emergency fund.
You're saving for a goal within the next one to five years.
You have extra cash sitting in a low-interest checking or traditional savings account.
You prioritize safety over higher potential investment returns.
You don't need to write checks or use the money for everyday spending.
An HYSA may not be the best choice if...
You're investing for retirement or another goal that's 10+ years away. Investing in a diversified portfolio has historically produced higher long-term returns, though with greater risk.
You won't need the money for a fixed period. If you can leave your savings untouched for several months or years, a certificate of deposit (CD) may offer a higher guaranteed yield.
You need frequent access to your money. A checking account is more convenient for paying bills and making everyday purchases.
How much interest will an HYSA earn by 2027?
If you want to supercharge your savings this year, consider a high-yield savings account (HYSA). Here's a look at how much an HYSA can earn through 2027 based on today's rates.

With deposit interest rates falling, you may be wondering if your high-yield savings account (HYSA) is still worth it. Here’s what to know.

Do high-yield savings account rates change often? And why do banks raise or lower their rates? Here’s what you should know.
Typically, high-yield savings accounts are perfectly safe. But you still need to take steps to protect your funds, including banking with a federally insured institution and avoiding fees.

articles.title: Federal judge slaps down Ghislaine Maxwell petition for new trial as ‘rambling,’ ‘meritless’
articles.summary: Judge Paul Engelmayer called Ghislaine Maxwell's post-conviction challenge "meritless" and "frivolous," finding trial evidence against her "overwhelming."
articles.body: A federal judge rejected Ghislaine Maxwell’s latest effort to overturn her conviction, blasting her petition as "lengthy and rambling" and finding her claims "all meritless" and "all or almost all" frivolous. U.S. District Judge Paul A. Engelmayer denied Maxwell’s post-conviction challenge in an opinion filed Monday in the Southern District of New York and made public Tuesday, writing that the evidence against the convicted Jeffrey Epstein associate at trial was "overwhelming." Maxwell, representing herself, had moved to vacate her conviction and 20-year prison sentence, alleging that her constitutional rights were violated at trial and sentencing. TODD BLANCHE SAYS 'NO CLOSED INVESTIGATIONS' IN EPSTEIN CASE, VOWS DOJ WILL PURSUE NEW SUSPECTS Engelmayer said the vast majority of her arguments were procedurally barred because she either raised and lost them on direct appeal or could have raised them earlier but did not. The judge also shot down Maxwell’s reliance on material released under the Epstein Files Transparency Act, finding that the purported new evidence did not support her claims. The supposedly "new" evidence was largely irrelevant to  Maxwell 's case, the judge said. FORMER ATTORNEY GENERAL PAM BONDI HAILS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S 'JUSTICE AND TRANSPARENCY' ON EPSTEIN FILES "To the extent it is relevant, far from exculpating her, it incriminates her or reinforces the correctness of the legal rulings Maxwell challenges," Engelmayer wrote. "The Court accordingly denies Maxwell’s petition," he concluded. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Maxwell was convicted in December 2021 on five felony counts stemming from her participation with Epstein in the sexual abuse of young girls over the course of a decade. Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy trial: Judge rejects mistrial plea after psychologist's Catholic faith remarks
articles.summary: US News: A judge has rejected a defence request for a mistrial in the case of Lindsay Clancy, who is accused of killing her three young children in Massachuset.
articles.body: A judge has rejected a defence request for a mistrial in the case of Lindsay Clancy, who is accused of killing her three young children in Massachusetts, after a prosecution psychologist brought her Catholic faith into his testimony.The ruling came as Clancy's closely watched triple-murder trial neared its conclusion, with closing arguments expected Wednesday, according to NBC News.Defence seeks mistrial over Catholic faith remarksForensic psychologist Kirk Heilbrun was testifying for the prosecution when he referred to Clancy's Roman Catholic upbringing while discussing her state of mind at the time of the killings.Heilbrun mentioned Clancy's statement that she told her children to âGo to Godâ before killing them and questioned her about Catholic teachings on suicide.The defence immediately objected, and attorney Kevin Reddington moved for a mistrial, accusing the prosecution of improperly introducing religion into the trial.Judge Sullivan rejected the mistrial request but ordered jurors to disregard Heilbrun's remarks about Clancy's faith and Catholic theology.âThe religion that the defendant was raised is absolutely an inappropriate area of testimony,â the judge was quoted as saying by CNN. He also instructed jurors not to consider the remarks.Psychologist questions psychosis claimHeilbrun's testimony otherwise focused on whether Clancy was experiencing psychosis when she killed her children, Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, at their Duxbury home in January 2023.He said Clancy claimed she heard a male voice telling her to kill herself and her children, but noted that she did not report hearing the voice before or after the killings.The psychologist said the account was more consistent with an intrusive thought than a command hallucination and described the killings as âaltruistic filicideâ â killing children out of a belief that they would suffer without the parent, CNN reported.Defence says postpartum psychosis left her unawareClancy, 36, has pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity to three counts of murder. She has admitted killing her children, but her defence says she was in the grip of severe postpartum mental illness and could not appreciate the wrongfulness of her actions.Prosecutors argue that while Clancy had mental health problems, she understood what she was doing and deliberately killed her children before attempting suicide.Closing arguments are expected Wednesday as the trial moves towards a verdict.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 7 hours for lip gloss, 2 hours for a croissant: Welcome to line culture, where flexing how long you waited is part of the fun
articles.summary: Waiting in line is cool again. For young people chasing viral products and experiences, the inconvenience may be part of what makes it special.
articles.body:
At 5:30 in the morning, Kristen and her sister arrived in Newport, Rhode Island, armed with a blanket, snacks and a suspicion that Hailey Bieber might show up. The 22-year-old had driven an hour from Connecticut for the first day of the summer pop-up from Rhode, a special event from Bieber's massively popular beauty brand, celebrating a seasonal drop . The doors wouldn't open until 11 a.m. Kristen had never done anything like this before and she expected the hours to drag. But that didn't end up being the case.

"We were just making friends with the people around us," she tells Yahoo. "It was really cool to hear everyone's story on why they were there, where they're coming from."

Even after the doors finally opened — five and a half hours after they arrived — Kristen was still about 40th in line and had another hour and a half to wait. But the waiting had begun to turn into something else.

Security handed out wristbands. Newport coffee shop Nitro Bar passed out caramelized banana lattes , a nod to a drink Bieber had talked about making at home. There were bingo cards with the chance to win free products. "The little surprises that came along the way got people so excited," says Kristen. "And that's when I was like, OK, waiting was worth it."

Kristen ended up nabbing a pocket bronzer, two lip liners and lip glosses, and an exclusive Newport Rhode hoodie. She returned again the next day and spent another six hours outside the pop-up, hoping Bieber would appear. (She didn't. But cinnamon rolls were passed around for attendees.)

Today's young people came of age in an era of one-click everything, where almost anything can be ordered to your doorstep in a matter of 48 hours. Given that fact, spending the better part of one (or two) days waiting outside a store sounds almost absurd.

Yet this summer, lines have solidified themselves as a recurring feature in the lives of young people chasing after trendy consumer products: they've formed outside beauty pop-ups and bakeries, artist activations, coffee and matcha shops and stores carrying the latest cult item. Getting the thing that you want, line enthusiasts say, is almost more special because you had to prove that you really wanted it.

The merchandise might be available elsewhere. But acquiring the thing isn't necessarily the point. "People don't wait in line for products anymore," Ryan Glick, founder of Coffee N' Clothes (CNC) , a brand-experience agency that produces more than 200 events a year, tells Yahoo. "They're waiting in line to be a part of a moment."

Glick has seen the phenomenon evolve from both sides of the rope. He started his company by organizing meet-ups for online communities and eventually grew it into a business that helps brands across fashion, beauty, entertainment and tech produce IRL experiences. "In a world where digital made everything available to everyone instantly, showing up is proof that you're physically there for something that mattered," he says.

There may also be something psychological happening as those hours tick by too, according to Derek D. Rucker , a professor of marketing at Northwestern University, who points to the concept of "effort justification" — the tendency to value something more once we've invested time or work into getting it. "The more effort we have to put into something, the more we justify it as, 'It must be worth it,'" Rucker tells Yahoo.

Kristen could've waited for the Rhode products she wanted to arrive at Sephora. But the pop-up offered something Sephora couldn't. "It's just a cooler experience when you go to an event for it," she said. With only two U.S. pop-up locations at the time, being able to attend one made her "feel special."

That distinction — between buying something and being there — runs through the line phenomenon.

When Valeria Rose, 23, recently returned to Los Angeles after attending college in Santa Barbara, she went to Ariana Grande's Eternal Sunshine experience in West Hollywood. She had seen TikToks of fans arriving at 6 a.m. and not getting inside until mid-afternoon, so she strategically went on a weekday. She still waited nearly three hours.

The fan event was cool — there was a photo booth and a flower-covered wall where fans could leave Grande notes. But more importantly, Valeria went with a friend who wanted to be there as much as she did. "Having someone to chat with honestly makes the time go faster," she tells Yahoo.

Growing up near the entertainment industry, Valeria is a veteran of line culture. She's met people waiting in line for concerts, meet-and-greets and pop-ups — some of those friendships lasted long after the line disappeared. Returning to that ritual after years away from L.A. also offered an unexpected connection to her younger self.

"It was pretty funny that on my first day back home, I was waiting in line," she says. "I felt so connected to my past self."

On vacation in Arizona, Elizabeth and her sister had an open day and kept seeing Sablé Boulangerie, a viral bakery in Gilbert, on their TikTok feeds. They decided to see what the hype was about and spent an hour and 37 minutes in line to get their hands on a selection of pastries and the bakery's internet-famous chocolate chip cookie.

Around them, people worked on laptops, played games and sat in chairs. Families and groups of friends waited together. Chef Will Porter, whose social media presence has helped make the bakery a destination, briefly "walked the line" with a cameraman and bodyguards.

Elizabeth started filming mostly because she was curious how long the wait would take. The resulting video got 50,000 views, when most of her posts typically draw around 500.

"If you post about standing in a line and say how long you stood in the line, people can't wait to tell you how dumb you are in the comments," says Elizabeth. "It drives engagement. It's essentially easy rage bait."

It creates a strategically efficient cycle: A viral place attracts a crowd. The crowd creates a line. People film the line because it is remarkable. The resulting content reaches more people, who then want to see what could possibly be worth waiting for.

It's a marketing jackpot. Whether you encounter it in person or watch it unfold on TikTok, you're seeing dozens of people weigh whether something is really that valuable in real time. Timothy D. Malefyt , a marketing professor at Fordham University, calls that "embodied social proof" and it naturally gives observers FOMO, the feeling that the people in line "apparently know something I don't."

There is, Elizabeth admits, "a bit of excitement to try something that's trending and see for yourself if it's actually good." Going also gives you something to talk about when other people inevitably ask, "Was it worth it?"

In her case, yes — with a caveat. She still thinks about Sablé's pain suisse. "The pastries truly were delicious," she says, "but I wouldn't stand in that line again."

Of course, people stood in lines long before TikTok. There were Black Friday doorbusters, concert ticket sales and Supreme drops. Glick remembers waiting outside Supreme — which was created as more of a community space than a traditional retail store — with his mom as a kid.

What has changed may be how many ordinary products can now be transformed into events — and how quickly social media can create a craze around them.

In Iowa, Anna T., 40, found herself waking up before dawn to hunt for NeeDoh squishy toys with her 11-year-old daughter. A local children's boutique would announce "drop" dates for harder-to-find designs, prompting customers to line up before opening.

The first time Anna went, she waited in the snow for roughly two hours. On another trip, she and her daughter arrived at 6:15 a.m. for a 9 a.m. opening. Eventually, Anna took her daughter and two friends at 5 a.m. By then, the wait had become an event of its own. "The store owner came out around 7:30 a.m. and had music," she tells Yahoo. "The kids were dancing, and it was a very fun and lively experience."

For Anna's daughter, the inconvenience was novel — and part of the appeal. "She told me she really wanted to because she has never waited in line to buy anything before and she said she wanted to experience that," says Anna. That struck her. "We've waited in lines for a ride, but never for a material thing."

In a childhood shaped by online shopping and instant gratification, even the hassle is part of the charm. "When something is easily accessible, we tend to think anyone could get it and that it's not as special as things that took work, energy, time or were scarce," Elizabeth Schwab , a professor in the Business Psychology Division at The Chicago School, tells Yahoo.

But the hours spent waiting can offer something else that clicking "buy now" can't: doing it with others. "We enjoy feeling like we belong; that we've found our people and our community," Schwab says.

That would explain why, for Anna, the NeeDohs themselves were almost beside the point. "I don't do it for the actual item," she says. "For my daughter, it was about getting the trendy new item, but I know these are memories that she will be able to talk about with her kids one day. And all of it is a reason for us to spend time together."

Valeria questions the appeal of standing around for something as fleeting as a celebrity-branded smoothie. Glick cautions that brands shouldn't manufacture lines simply to appeal popular — a badly managed wait can just as easily backfire, he says.

And even the people willing to queue for hours know how irrational it can look from the outside. Perhaps that's what makes the line work.

Convenience has stripped away much of the friction that once surrounded buying something. The line puts some of it back, but with friends, anticipation, exclusivity and a story attached.

The most telling thing about this summer of lines may be that Anna's daughter didn't simply want the NeeDoh. She really wanted to wait for it.
paragraphs: At 5:30 in the morning, Kristen and her sister arrived in Newport, Rhode Island, armed with a blanket, snacks and a suspicion that Hailey Bieber might show up. The 22-year-old had driven an hour from Connecticut for the first day of the summer pop-up from Rhode, a special event from Bieber's massively popular beauty brand, celebrating a seasonal drop . The doors wouldn't open until 11 a.m. Kristen had never done anything like this before and she expected the hours to drag. But that didn't end up being the case.
"We were just making friends with the people around us," she tells Yahoo. "It was really cool to hear everyone's story on why they were there, where they're coming from."

Even after the doors finally opened — five and a half hours after they arrived — Kristen was still about 40th in line and had another hour and a half to wait. But the waiting had begun to turn into something else.

Security handed out wristbands. Newport coffee shop Nitro Bar passed out caramelized banana lattes , a nod to a drink Bieber had talked about making at home. There were bingo cards with the chance to win free products. "The little surprises that came along the way got people so excited," says Kristen. "And that's when I was like, OK, waiting was worth it."

Kristen ended up nabbing a pocket bronzer, two lip liners and lip glosses, and an exclusive Newport Rhode hoodie. She returned again the next day and spent another six hours outside the pop-up, hoping Bieber would appear. (She didn't. But cinnamon rolls were passed around for attendees.)

Today's young people came of age in an era of one-click everything, where almost anything can be ordered to your doorstep in a matter of 48 hours. Given that fact, spending the better part of one (or two) days waiting outside a store sounds almost absurd.

Yet this summer, lines have solidified themselves as a recurring feature in the lives of young people chasing after trendy consumer products: they've formed outside beauty pop-ups and bakeries, artist activations, coffee and matcha shops and stores carrying the latest cult item. Getting the thing that you want, line enthusiasts say, is almost more special because you had to prove that you really wanted it.

The merchandise might be available elsewhere. But acquiring the thing isn't necessarily the point. "People don't wait in line for products anymore," Ryan Glick, founder of Coffee N' Clothes (CNC) , a brand-experience agency that produces more than 200 events a year, tells Yahoo. "They're waiting in line to be a part of a moment."

Glick has seen the phenomenon evolve from both sides of the rope. He started his company by organizing meet-ups for online communities and eventually grew it into a business that helps brands across fashion, beauty, entertainment and tech produce IRL experiences. "In a world where digital made everything available to everyone instantly, showing up is proof that you're physically there for something that mattered," he says.

There may also be something psychological happening as those hours tick by too, according to Derek D. Rucker , a professor of marketing at Northwestern University, who points to the concept of "effort justification" — the tendency to value something more once we've invested time or work into getting it. "The more effort we have to put into something, the more we justify it as, 'It must be worth it,'" Rucker tells Yahoo.

Kristen could've waited for the Rhode products she wanted to arrive at Sephora. But the pop-up offered something Sephora couldn't. "It's just a cooler experience when you go to an event for it," she said. With only two U.S. pop-up locations at the time, being able to attend one made her "feel special."
That distinction — between buying something and being there — runs through the line phenomenon.

When Valeria Rose, 23, recently returned to Los Angeles after attending college in Santa Barbara, she went to Ariana Grande's Eternal Sunshine experience in West Hollywood. She had seen TikToks of fans arriving at 6 a.m. and not getting inside until mid-afternoon, so she strategically went on a weekday. She still waited nearly three hours.

The fan event was cool — there was a photo booth and a flower-covered wall where fans could leave Grande notes. But more importantly, Valeria went with a friend who wanted to be there as much as she did. "Having someone to chat with honestly makes the time go faster," she tells Yahoo.

Growing up near the entertainment industry, Valeria is a veteran of line culture. She's met people waiting in line for concerts, meet-and-greets and pop-ups — some of those friendships lasted long after the line disappeared. Returning to that ritual after years away from L.A. also offered an unexpected connection to her younger self.
"It was pretty funny that on my first day back home, I was waiting in line," she says. "I felt so connected to my past self."

On vacation in Arizona, Elizabeth and her sister had an open day and kept seeing Sablé Boulangerie, a viral bakery in Gilbert, on their TikTok feeds. They decided to see what the hype was about and spent an hour and 37 minutes in line to get their hands on a selection of pastries and the bakery's internet-famous chocolate chip cookie.

Around them, people worked on laptops, played games and sat in chairs. Families and groups of friends waited together. Chef Will Porter, whose social media presence has helped make the bakery a destination, briefly "walked the line" with a cameraman and bodyguards.
Elizabeth started filming mostly because she was curious how long the wait would take. The resulting video got 50,000 views, when most of her posts typically draw around 500.

"If you post about standing in a line and say how long you stood in the line, people can't wait to tell you how dumb you are in the comments," says Elizabeth. "It drives engagement. It's essentially easy rage bait."

It creates a strategically efficient cycle: A viral place attracts a crowd. The crowd creates a line. People film the line because it is remarkable. The resulting content reaches more people, who then want to see what could possibly be worth waiting for.

It's a marketing jackpot. Whether you encounter it in person or watch it unfold on TikTok, you're seeing dozens of people weigh whether something is really that valuable in real time. Timothy D. Malefyt , a marketing professor at Fordham University, calls that "embodied social proof" and it naturally gives observers FOMO, the feeling that the people in line "apparently know something I don't."

There is, Elizabeth admits, "a bit of excitement to try something that's trending and see for yourself if it's actually good." Going also gives you something to talk about when other people inevitably ask, "Was it worth it?"
In her case, yes — with a caveat. She still thinks about Sablé's pain suisse. "The pastries truly were delicious," she says, "but I wouldn't stand in that line again."

Of course, people stood in lines long before TikTok. There were Black Friday doorbusters, concert ticket sales and Supreme drops. Glick remembers waiting outside Supreme — which was created as more of a community space than a traditional retail store — with his mom as a kid.

Eventually, Anna took her daughter and two friends at 5 a.m. By then, the wait had become an event of its own. "The store owner came out around 7:30 a.m. and had music," she tells Yahoo. "The kids were dancing, and it was a very fun and lively experience."

For Anna's daughter, the inconvenience was novel — and part of the appeal. articles.title: In 2022, CaseOh was mowing lawns and making TikToks after work; two years later, he won Content Creator of the Year
articles.summary: US Streamers News: Case Dylan Baker, known online as CaseOh, had a pretty normal working life before the internet changed everything for him. He was doing maintenance wo.
articles.body: Case Dylan Baker, known online as CaseOh, had a pretty normal working life before the internet changed everything for him. He was doing maintenance work with his father in rural Arkansas, handling things like plumbing and mowing lawns. Streaming was something he had wanted to do since his early teens, inspired by creators like Nadeshot and the early OpTic Gaming scene. But his first attempts at making videos did not really go anywhere. Then came September 2022. Baker started uploading batches of funny NBA 2K23 clips to TikTok, timing them around the release of new versions of the game. The move worked way faster than expected. Within 48 hours, he had gained more than 10,000 followers, and on September 11, he went live on Twitch for the first time. Just two years later, the same creator was standing at The Game Awards, winning Content Creator of the Year.CaseOhâs first big break came from NBA 2K23 TikToksThe TikTok strategy became the first real turning point. Instead of slowly building an audience, Baker pushed several short, energetic clips around NBA 2K23. The sudden follower growth gave him a reason to move those viewers toward Twitch.His early streams were not exactly running on a perfect setup either. Because of limited internet infrastructure in rural Arkansas, he famously had to use a mobile hotspot for some broadcasts. Still, the growth kept coming. By November 2022, less than two months after starting, he received an invitation to the Twitch Partner Program.His audience helped turn CaseOh into a variety streamerNBA 2K was only the beginning. Baker eventually moved into indie games, simulators, low-budget horror titles and Roblox. Games like Contraband Police and Supermarket Simulator became part of the variety format that defined his streams.A huge part of the appeal was his interaction with chat. Viewers regularly threw food-related jokes at him, including lines like âBuilt like a 1x1 Lego pieceâ and âCase-a-dilla.â His mock-rage reactions and quick ban-hammer moments became a recognizable part of the streams.CaseOh went from Arkansas maintenance work to The Game AwardsOn December 12, 2024, the journey reached its biggest point yet. At The Game Awards at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles, Baker won Content Creator of the Year.He beat a field that included Usada Pekora, Typical Gamer, Techno Gamerz and IlloJuan. He had also picked up multiple Best Variety Streamer awards at The Streamer Awards.For Baker, the win carried a very specific meaning. He had gone from long days of blue-collar maintenance work in a small Arkansas town to one of the biggest creator awards in gaming. His victory speeches repeatedly returned to that background, showing that the entire jump happened while he stayed rooted in the same story: an average guy from Arkansas finding a massive audience by being authentic and consistent.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Lake America? Trump's latest salvo against Canada takes ties to uncharted waters
articles.summary: US News: TOI Correspondent From Washington: US-Canada relations are in danger of tipping into Niagara Falls, which straddles both countries, after MAGA boss Do.
articles.body: TOI Correspondent From Washington: US-Canada relations are in danger of tipping into Niagara Falls, which straddles both countries, after MAGA boss Donald Trump threatened to rename Lake Ontario, into which the storied waterfall empties -- as Lake America. Ontarioâs pugnacious premier Doug Ford in turn effectively said "bring it on," warning of cutting electricity exports to the US and restricting critical minerals such as nickel and uranium.The latest installment of the increasingly surreal trade war between neighbors who have the longest peaceful and unmilitarized border in the world (8891 kms) came after Trump decided that if Canada will not fall in line economically, he will mess with it cartographically.âThe United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we donât expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer,â Trump posted on his social media account, with a separate post showing the change in nomenclature.Having already rechristened the Gulf of Mexico the âGulf of America,â the US President appears to be discovering that the North American atlas is offering more opportunities for rebranding, with Venezuela and Cuba possibly next in line. But jokes aside, there is a distinctly serious undertone to the developments where U.S ties with two benign neighbors is turning toxic.Canada on Tuesday announced retaliatory tariffs covering more than 700 American products worth roughly $20 billion after Trump wielded his tariff bazooka first. The measures, due to take effect Sept. 8, include tariffs of 15%, 25% and 50% on American exports ranging from steel and dairy to appliances, seafood and cosmetics. Ottawa also announced a C$7.5 billion support package for industries hit by the dispute.The latest confrontation follows the collapse of trade talks after Canadian PM Mark Carney rejected U.S. demands he claimed went beyond trade, touching Canadian cultural and French-language protections. Trump, for his part, insists Canada has been âripping offâ America for decades and says the country is âeasily the most difficult and unreasonableâ trading partner, even as he denied having problems with Canadaâs French heritage.âI would never interfere with Canadians speaking French! In fact, I have never even thought of doing such a stupid thing. This lie was made up by a weak and ineffective Prime Minister in an attempt to gain political support, which he has totally lost, from the people of Quebec. I love French Canadians!â Trump wrote.There is a delicious historical irony to Trump's proposed renaming campaign. âOntarioâ is derived from the Iroquoian word kanadario, generally translated as âsparkling water.â âCanadaâ itself is said to come from the Huron-Iroquois word kanata, meaning âvillageâ or âsettlement.â And âAmericaâ? That name wasn't exactly minted in Philadelphia. It came from Amerigo Vespucci, the Italian explorer, with German cartographer Martin WaldseemÃ¼ller first putting âAmericaâ on his 1507 map.So, historically speaking, the names of both countries and the lake in question are products of Indigenous languages and European cartography. Nobody involved in today's quarrel can quite claim to have invented the labels, and the geopolitical equivalent of âfinders, keepersâ is therefore on rather shaky historical ground.The larger casualty from the spat may be something less easily renamed: the extraordinary ease with which the US and Canada once conducted business. For generations, the two countries were the diplomatic equivalent of the neighbors who borrowed each other's lawnmowers and never bothered with keeping the score. Their economies became so intertwined that auto parts can cross the border repeatedly before a finished vehicle emerges; energy, minerals, agriculture and manufacturing operate through deeply integrated supply chains.Trump's aggressive trade strategy has shaken that comfortable arrangement. Carney has said Canada will return to negotiations if Washington changes its approach, but the relationship has already entered unfamiliar territory. America and Canada used to have the world's longest undefended border. Now the only thing crossing it freely may be heated words.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Autistic DJ befriended at Boomtown Fair offered 'dream' set
articles.summary: Adam, 23, has been asked to play a DJ set at the music event next year after his story went viral.
articles.body:
An autistic man whose story about being befriended by strangers when he attended his first-ever festival alone went viral has been invited to play a DJ set next year.

Adam James, 23, from High Wycombe in Buckinghamshire, "realised his dream" after he made friends with a group of festival-goers who invited him to camp with them at Boomtown Fair in Hampshire.

The lifelong music fan and aspiring drum and bass DJ has now been offered a set at the festival in 2027.

Adam's dad, Andy, whose social media post thanking the "lads from Bristol" who took Adam under their wing has been seen by millions, said he had seen his "son's dreams come true".

"It's made me really, really proud... Adam's over the moon," he added.

The festival's co-founder, Luke Mitchell, commented on a BBC video to say the story had "circled around the Boomtown office with absolute joy".

"Stories like this are why festivals are so incredibly important," he said, before asking Andy: "Can we fix up a DJ set for Adam next year?"

A spokesperson for Boomtown Fair confirmed that they had asked Adam to play a set, with the stage and timings to be announced once programming for next year's event has begun.

Adam, also known as Adzo to his friends, previously said he had been nervous for his first festival experience, but everything had changed after meeting the group when they asked him if he had a mallet to help build their tents.

"I wasn't very confident in myself, but as soon as I was with them, I was fine," he said. "They could have just ignored me, but the fact they saw I was on my own and took me in was just amazing."

Following the viral post, which has been shared and liked by thousands of people, Adam was reunited with the group at the Trident Pub in Bristol and was booked for several gigs.

Since his story has been shared online, Adam has been inundated with offers from DJs and clubs to come to their events and play at their venues, and has even been invited by the Pete Tong Academy to join a DJing course.

Andy told the BBC the reaction had been "absolutely amazing" to see, particularly after Adam had faced cruel comments online in the past.

"He's become very resilient, but he's such a lovely bloke," his dad said. "It means so much to me and his Mum too."

articles.title: What drives the price of gold?
articles.summary: Learn what drives the price of gold, including supply and demand, interest rates, the U.S. dollar, and physical demand
articles.body:
Some offers on this page are from advertisers who pay us, which may affect which products we write about, but not our recommendations. See our Advertiser Disclosure .

Gold doesn't rise or fall because of a single economic event. Its price reflects the decisions of millions of investors, central banks, manufacturers, jewelers, and others around the world. Those decisions are shaped by changing economic conditions and future expectations.

Understanding what drives the price of gold means learning how multiple forces interact. Sometimes they reinforce one another. Sometimes they pull in opposite directions.

That's why different headlines can describe the same market move from different angles.

Every second the global gold market is open, buyers and sellers are negotiating a price — but they're not all buying gold for the same reason.

An investor may be looking to diversify a portfolio. A jewelry manufacturer may need gold for finished products. A technology company may use it in electronic components. A central bank may be increasing its reserves. Another investor may believe interest rates are about to fall.

Each enters the market with a different objective, but together, their buying and selling help determine the market price.

That's what makes gold different from many other assets. Gold serves as an investment, a reserve asset, a consumer product, and an industrial material. Because it serves several purposes at once, demand comes from many participants responding to different economic conditions simultaneously — not from a single type of buyer or economic trend.

How much gold would $1 million buy at different points in history?

Like any market, gold prices are shaped by supply and demand. What makes gold different is how each side of that equation changes.

Gold supply grows relatively slowly. New mines can take years to develop, and much of the gold ever mined is still available through existing holdings or recycled metal.

Investor interest may increase during periods of market uncertainty. Jewelry demand may rise during periods of strong consumer spending or seasonal buying. Because supply changes gradually while demand can shift quickly, demand changes often have a greater effect on short-term price movements. Unlike oil or agricultural commodities, most of the gold ever mined still exists today, making changes in demand especially important when explaining why gold prices move.

Supply sets the stage. Demand often explains short-term movements.

Gold doesn't pay interest or dividends. That means investors often compare it with assets that do, such as savings accounts, certificates of deposit (CDs), or bonds. Economists call this tradeoff opportunity cost — the value of what you give up by choosing one investment instead of another.

For example, if a savings account pays 5% interest, some investors may decide that a guaranteed return is more attractive than holding an asset that doesn't produce income. Others may still prefer gold because of concerns about inflation, market volatility, or the economy.

Markets also respond to expected interest rates — not only current rates. Central bank policy announcements, inflation reports, employment data, and comments from policymakers can all shape those expectations.

Because financial markets are forward-looking, gold prices sometimes move before interest rates actually change.

Higher interest rates can increase the opportunity cost of holding gold, while changing expectations about future rates can shape gold prices even before policy changes occur.

Gold is often described as a hedge against inflation because many investors believe it can help preserve purchasing power over long periods. That belief alone can increase interest in gold when inflation concerns begin to grow.

You'll also hear the term inflation expectations . Simply put, it's what people think inflation will do in the future. If consumers and investors expect prices for everyday goods to keep rising, some may adjust their portfolios before inflation data fully reflects those expectations.

What investors expect can matter just as much as what's happening today. Interest rates, the U.S. dollar, investor sentiment, and other economic forces also help shape the market.

Gold is generally priced in U.S. dollars on international markets. That means changes in the dollar's value can affect buyers worldwide.

For example, if the U.S. dollar strengthens against the euro, a buyer in Europe may have to spend more euros to purchase the same ounce of gold — even if the dollar price hasn't changed. That higher cost can reduce demand from international buyers.

If the dollar weakens, the opposite may occur. Gold can become cheaper for buyers using other currencies, potentially boosting demand.

Currency movements can influence global buying activity, but they rarely explain price movements on their own.

The first is through monetary policy. Decisions about interest rates — and even signals about future policy — can shape investor expectations for inflation, economic growth, and borrowing costs. As discussed earlier, those expectations may affect demand for gold.

The second is through gold purchases. Many central banks hold physical gold as part of their official reserves. When they buy or sell gold, those transactions directly affect global market demand.

These are related but separate drivers. A central bank may signal future interest rate changes without buying additional gold. Likewise, it may increase its gold reserves without making a significant change to monetary policy.

That's why news about central banks can move gold prices for different reasons. Sometimes investors are reacting to policy. Other times, they're reacting to physical gold purchases.

Not every change in gold prices is driven by economic data. Sometimes, investor psychology plays an important role.

During periods of financial market volatility, geopolitical tensions, or broader economic uncertainty, some investors become more interested in assets they believe may help preserve value if other investments decline.

That doesn't mean uncertainty always pushes gold prices higher . Different events produce different market reactions, and investors don't all respond the same way.

Gold prices don't move because of one economic indicator or a single news event.

Instead, they reflect the interaction of supply and demand, interest rates, inflation expectations, the strength of the U.S. dollar, central bank policy, investor sentiment, and other market forces.

Understanding those relationships won't help you predict short-term price movements. But it can make them easier to interpret — and explain why headlines often point to different reasons for the same market movement.

articles.title: Spanish government says sorry to people of Ceuta for migrant crisis
articles.summary: Several thousand migrants remain in the enclave after a mass crossing from Morocco in late July.
articles.body:
The Spanish government has apologised to the people of Ceuta for the migrant crisis that has affected the city for weeks and it has unveiled plans to overhaul the country's immigration laws.

"I want to apologise to all those who may have felt, or who even still feel, abandoned or not sufficiently cared for," Defence Minister Margarita Robles told a parliamentary committee.

"I have witnessed first-hand your feelings of anxiety, of abandonment, of lack of safety."

At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta, a Spanish exclave in North Africa on 30 and 31 July.

Most of the migrants swam around the border fence and at least 100 people died during the mass crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor, Juan Jesús Vivas.

The vast majority of the migrants returned to Morocco within hours of their arrival, but several thousand remain in Ceuta, many of them children, and most sleeping rough on beaches or streets.

The Socialist government of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has been under mounting pressure to resolve the situation, with many residents and the local authorities in Ceuta, which has a population of 84,000, complaining that it is unsustainable.

The Sánchez government has now declared a situation of interest for national security in the city, centralising management of the crisis. Territorial Policy Minister Ángel Víctor Torres has been tasked with co-ordinating the response, relieving the Ceuta local government of that responsibility.

Coinciding with the government's moves and Robles's parliamentary appearance – the first by ministers on this issue over the coming days – changes were also announced to migration and asylum legislation.

Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said the reforms would seek to ensure Spain that was fully in line with new EU regulations and that its process was "orderly, efficient, and... [provided] all possible guarantees".

It will include limiting to three days the amount of time an undocumented migrant can spend undergoing medical, biometric and legal evaluation on arrival – EU regulations allow this period to last up to seven days.

The reforms will also create a two-speed system for processing asylum requests, in theory accelerating cases deemed urgent.

However, the information provided by government ministers has left some questions unanswered.

Robles told parliament that agents of the CNI intelligence service had shared information about a possible imminent migrant crossing with security forces shortly before it happened, but Grande-Marlaska appeared to contradict her.

"There was no report that hinted that on 30 July what eventually happened was going to happen," he said. Robles later said that the information had not been conveyed via a report.

Sánchez has blamed traffickers and social media activity for the mass crossing.

However, many others have pointed the finger at Morocco, which in the past has been accused of using the borders with Ceuta and its sister city Melilla to pressure Madrid or the EU on political issues.

Instagram accounts fuelling Ceuta crisis with paid advice for help to cross

Morocco detains dozens of migrants trying to cross into Ceuta, reports say

"The crisis in Ceuta didn't begin on 30 July," said Esther Muñoz of the conservative People's Party (PP), as she questioned Robles in parliament.

"It's been brewing for years and you know it, because you know that [the Moroccan authorities] have spent years sizing us up, sizing up our ability to respond and our willingness to do so."

The crisis has raised concerns in Spain about Moroccan claims to Ceuta and Melilla.

Last week, Moroccan Justice Minister Abdellatif Ouahbi spoke of his country's "historical and geographical right" to the cities and proposed talks with Spain on the issue.

Robles told the parliamentary committee she not would not allow "any minister from any government, in this case Morocco, to question the Spanish status of Ceuta and Melilla".

EU commends Spain's 'swift response' to Ceuta migrant crisis

articles.title: Massachusetts cuts Flock ties, seeks charges after officer accused of tracking ex-girlfriend
articles.summary: "Using that access for a personal purpose is a serious violation of that trust, and it is a crime."
articles.body:
An automated license plate reader program in Stow, Massachusetts, is being dismantled after investigators said a police officer used law enforcement databases for personal reasons.

The Lowell Sun reported that officer Jason Rogers, who served as a detective and acting sergeant, is facing both termination proceedings and potential criminal charges.

Town officials said Rogers obtained information about someone identified as his former girlfriend. Police said the matter began June 18, when a complaint was filed.

The paper noted that Rogers was placed on paid administrative leave within three hours and stripped of access to department systems.

Police said the internal affairs inquiry found that several database searches had no legitimate law enforcement purpose. Investigators counted at least five instances in which Rogers accessed Criminal Offender Record Information through the Criminal Justice Information Services system, along with vehicle searches run on multiple dates.

"Law enforcement officers are entrusted with access to sensitive information solely so they can perform their official duties and protect the public," Police Chief Michael Sallese told the Sun. "Using that access for a personal purpose is a serious violation of that trust, and it is a crime."

The department said the investigation found several violations, including database policy breaches, false or unsubstantiated search reasons, failure to comply with written orders, misuse of official position, and conduct unbecoming an officer.

The paper reported that Stow officials removed the last Flock automated license plate reader still operating in the town because of the incident.

Before using similar technology again, the Stow Police Department told the Sun it needs stronger safeguards, clearer rules, and better oversight. Even though plate reader data has helped solve crimes and locate missing people, its misuse is sparking nationwide backlash.

When used correctly, tools such as camera networks, automated searches, and large-scale data systems can help optimize traffic flow, improve public services, and support cleaner energy systems by helping utilities balance electricity demand.

At the same time, AI-related computing can consume large amounts of electricity and water, strain the power grid, and create security and privacy risks when used in the wrong way.

Following the investigation, the Stow Police Department sent the matter to the Middlesex County District Attorney's Office in order to seek charges.

Sallese also provided the full internal affairs report to the Massachusetts Peace Officer Standards and Training Commission, which the Sun said could decide what action to take regarding Rogers' certification to work as a police officer.

At the policy level, Sallese plans to bring a revised plate reader policy to the Select Board for future consideration. Officials said it would define when the technology could be used, require supervisory approval before use, and impose extensive logging and reporting requirements.

"The actions of one individual do not represent the values or conduct we expect from the good and dedicated members of the Stow Police Department," Town Administrator Denise M. Dembkoski told the paper.

articles.title: Woman, 51, Dies After an 8-Hour Plastic Surgery Procedure
articles.summary: A 51-year-old woman has died after undergoing extensive plastic surgery for her face and neck. Andreia Vieira Gaspar had saved up for years for her “dream” m...
articles.body:
A 51-year-old woman has died after undergoing extensive plastic surgery for her face and neck.

Andreia Vieira Gaspar had saved up for years for her "dream" mix of six plastic surgery procedures, The U.S. Sun reported on Monday. The combination of procedures cost around £17,000, or $23,000.

Gaspar died only hours after undergoing the eight-hour procedure on Aug. 12.

Gaspar, a businesswoman from Brazil, had lived in Spain for five years but flew to her home country to undergo plastic surgery at Hospital Ankar in Goiânia.

Her operation included a deep-plane facelift and a blepharoplasty, also known as an eyelid lift, during which surgeons remove fat and excess skin from the eyelids.

She also underwent a forehead lift, also known as a brow lift, neck liposuction, and bony genioplasty : a surgery to reshape the chin.

Gaspar's plastic surgery also included nanofat injections. This usually involves the surgeon harvesting the patient's fat, purifying it, and injecting it back into her face to improve skin texture and diminish the appearance of fine lines.

According to her family, Gaspar's health deteriorated quickly after she left the hospital, and she experienced extreme pain.

Her sister, Djiane Vieira, told Brazilian TV station TV Anhanguera that Gaspar's tongue swelled so much she was unable to close her mouth, and she struggled to breathe, according to The Daily Mail .

Vieira claimed to have texted her sister's medical team telling them her sister was "dying." The family also claimed that the hospital did not have an intensive care unit or ambulance available.

When the medics arrived, they were unable to save Gaspar.

According to her family, a medical report listed Gaspar's cause of death as acute thrombosis and pulmonary infarction. Acute thrombosis refers to a blood clot that blocks blood flow, and pulmonary infarction refers to the death of lung tissue when its blood supply is cut off.

The Goiás Public Prosecutor's Office has asked for a police investigation to be opened into possible involuntary manslaughter, according to The U.S. Sun.

According to the outlet, the doctor who performed Gaspar's plastic surgeries, Dr. Lessandro Martins, said he "sympathizes with the pain of her family," but is confident "the investigation will demonstrate that the care provided was appropriate".

Hospital Ankar's lawyer, Cristiene Pereira Couto, told the outlet: "The patient received immediate emergency treatment, with medical and nursing staff providing care and taking the necessary measures in response to her condition."

The attorney also said that once the emergency happened, the patient was attended to immediately. "She was promptly attended to by the staff present, who used the necessary hospital facilities and carried out the appropriate emergency measures."

The hospital also said Gaspar's pre-surgery evaluation was performed externally.

articles.title: Boston Symphony Orchestra and musicians agree to 3-year deal that avoids possible strike
articles.summary: The Boston Symphony Orchestra and its musicians ratified a three-year contract Tuesday, avoiding what could have been the first strike in the ensemble’s 145-...
articles.body:
BOSTON (AP) — The Boston Symphony Orchestra and its musicians ratified a three-year contract Tuesday, avoiding what could have been the first strike in the ensemble's 145-year history.

The orchestra and management have had strained relations since BSO decided in March to force out music director Andris Nelsons next summer after 13 seasons. The prior contract was set to expire last Sunday and was extended for 48 hours.

"This agreement marks an important step toward a more collaborative future for the BSO," orchestra management, trustees, the Boston Musicians' Association, the BSO Players Committee and management said in a joint statement released by the BSO. "It creates a precedent-setting partnership between musicians and management in artistic planning and centers excellence across all the work we do on our stages and in our communities. It also establishes a truly collaborative process in the search for our next music director."

"We are one institution of musicians, staff, and boards, committed to working together in partnership to advance our artistic mission, inspire audiences, and serve Boston, the Berkshires and beyond," the statement added.

BSO musicians and many audience members were angered by the decision in March to end the tenure of Nelsons, a five-time Grammy award winner.

"While the contract is an important first step, nothing else has been resolved," the BSO Patron Action Network said in a statement. "Andris Nelsons has not been reinstated as music director. CEO Chad Smith has still failed to provide any transparency around his future vision for the BSO, while stonewalling the dialogue that is essential to rebuilding trust with musicians, donors, patrons, and subscribers."

Smith said in a statement the deal "deepens our collaboration with the musicians and strengthens their role in the artistic planning process."

"The agreement guarantees the musicians a meaningful role engaging collaborators and planning repertoire that ensures artistic excellence," BMA president David Rufino said in a statement.

BSO Players Committee Chair Todd Seeber added "the agreement guarantees the musicians a critically enhanced role in the engagement of titled conductors, including the music director."

The orchestra's season is scheduled to open Sept. 17.

articles.title: The backlash Pride faces from inside and outside the LGBT community
articles.summary: Big companies used to go out of their way to support Pride. Now, there's a nervousness in the air, Darren Milby writes
articles.body:
Matt left Crewe as soon as he could, aged 18, feeling that he wasn't accepted as a young gay man. The only LGBT scene to mention was a tiny, makeshift bar behind a curtain in the back of an out-of-town pub.

He left in 2015, but this June found himself returning home, for Crewe Pride.

For Matt, it was a significant homecoming. "It really took me back to when I was a kid growing up here, trying to navigate my identity. It felt so important to be there and see how a town that wasn't particularly welcomingâ¦ has changed and flourished."

For many, these small, community Pride events feel a world away from the huge celebrations in the UK's largest cities.

But Matt's happy weekend in Crewe masks a growing culture war over Pride. Over the last few years, a number of councils have withdrawn their support for Pride festivals, while some big brands - perhaps nervous about being seen as too "woke" - have become hesitant to associate themselves with them. On top of all that, there's a long-running complaint from some LGBT campaigners that Pride has become overly commercialised; while the argument over trans issues has also made matters more fraught.

It's leading some to ask: what future do Pride events have?

Pride started as a protest, with Britain's first official Pride march in London in 1972. Homosexuality was illegal in the UK until 1967, and LGBT people lost jobs and housing because of their sexuality, while police forces frequently targeted the community with raids and surveillance that made everyday life precarious.

In Manchester, Pride started small in 1985. A bringâandâbuy sale on Canal Street was organised to raise money to spruce up the rather drab-looking hospital ward treating those with HIV and Aids at the height of the epidemic.

Little did those early attendees realise how big Manchester Pride would become: a four-day, city centre extravaganza over the August bank holiday weekend, with colourful floats, loud music, and every inch of pavement filled with enthusiastic spectators dressed to the nines, streaked with rainbow face paint.

By 2019, the event had outgrown the city's famous Gay Village. That year's headline act, American superstar Ariana Grande, performed in a purpose-built stage in another part of Manchester - for a premium ticket price. It prompted criticism, and the organisers of Manchester Pride would later come under fire for ending funding for various charities (including an HIV charity, and a scheme that distributed free condoms).

The company behind Manchester Pride went into voluntary liquidation last year, owing more than Â£1m to suppliers and performers, including Nelly Furtado. Since its collapse, local businesses and charities have created a not-for-profit group - Manchester Village Pride - with the aim of organising a much cheaper festival more rooted in the community.

Carl Austin-Behan, who is helping to organise this year's scaled-back event, says he's been "frustrated for a number of years" by the direction of Manchester Pride. "When things were being taken out of the village, that was the first sign that things were going in the wrong directionâ¦ It should be about the community. We certainly don't need to be spending the amount of money that was spent on Manchester Pride."

And Manchester's problems aren't isolated. London Pride has faced criticism for feeling overly corporate and overcrowded; Brighton has struggled with the financial burden of staging largeâscale concerts and policing. Against that backdrop, smaller events like Crewe seem to be the direction many Prides are going in 2026.

But the political winds have also changed - with seemingly less corporate enthusiasm for diversity and inclusion initiatives.

Phil Douglas, organiser of Newcastle Pride, says: "There is a general nervousness from organisations and companies to be front and centre in their support. We see some wanting to still support us but not wanting their logo attachedâ¦ they don't want the backlash which is right there ready in the online community. It's quite a complex time to navigate support for Prides as a whole."

A few years ago, you couldn't go on social media in June - known as "Pride month" - without seeing what felt like every corporate logo incorporating the Pride flag. Critics called it "rainbowâwashing", arguing that the displays of solidarity were more about marketing than meaningful action.

But now, according to Guardian analysis, the corporate presence has been waning. Last year, mentions of Pride on social media by the UK's 10 biggest listed or headquartered companies had fallen by 92% compared with 2023 - a drop that suggests brands are pulling back from overt LGBT messaging.

"There has been a general rowing back of corporate support for LGBT causes globally," says Paul Martin, chief executive of the LGBT Foundation charity. "We've seen that with politics changing in some countries and diversity and inclusion being seen as too wokeâ¦ We don't get support from some quarters like we used to.

"And that has played out with Pride festivals as well. Corporate funding has been pulled back and that has caused a real challenge for Pride organisers to balance the books."

A survey by the pollster Ipsos found that the share of British adults who want companies and brands to promote LGBT rights dipped from 52% in 2021 to 44% this year.

In Liverpool, Merseyside Police did not take part in the city's Pride parade last year after legal advice warned that uniformed participation by a public body could breach rules on political impartiality.

This summer, firefighters and police again stayed away: Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service said it was taking a "pragmatic approach" following a High Court ruling that found officers in the northâeast should not have been allowed to join a Pride event. West Midlands Ambulance Service also withdrew from Birmingham Pride on similar legal advice.

Back in May's local elections in England, Reform UK won power on 14 councils, adding to the 10 they already controlled. Last month, the party's leader, Nigel Farage, said he is "fine" with Pride events going ahead but did not want local authorities to promote them.

A few weeks after taking power in Durham last year, the town's new Reform administration removed a rainbow flag from the council headquarters. Councillors also withdrew their funding contribution of Â£2,500 for Durham Pride. In the Merseyside town of St Helens, meanwhile, the Reform council leader instructed officials to cease engagement with all aspects of Pride; the council also removed displays celebrating the festival from libraries.

Explaining the cuts to funding, Reform's Darren Grimes, deputy leader of Durham Council, says: "I feel that we've moved away from that laudable aim of gay equality. We achieved same-sex marriage and that was the final frontier."

Durham Pride organiser Mel Metcalf says taking the flag down made LGBT people in the community "feel unwelcome". The festival did still take place; organisers said it was their "biggest" year ever, after raising around Â£25,000 from individual donors and trade unions.

As well as Reform's approach, the new Conservative council leader in Enfield, north London, has said they will only fly certain flags outside Enfield Civic Centre - and the rainbow flag is not one of them.

Debate around trans rights is also fuelling the Pride culture war. Some gay and lesbian people who describe themselves as "gender critical" - and whose beliefs mean they're sceptical of some of the aims of the trans rights movement - say they feel sidelined by Pride; while some trans people say they no longer feel safe attending.

A lesbian woman who describes herself as gender critical, and did not want to be named, told me she no longer attends Pride because she thinks it has become dominated by a focus on trans issues.

Grimes, one of Reform's highest-profile gay members, argues that Pride has moved away from its focus on gay equality and become bound up with the wider gender identity debate: "You've slain the dragon in the pursuit of equality and now all you are left with is a few rambling sheep." He says that "public subsidy" for LGBT issues has become a "cash cow" that fuels "narratives of victimhood".

For some, the focus on trans rights is a reason to step back from Pride; for others, it underscores why events like Sparkle matter.

Sparkle is the UK's biggest transgender celebration. It takes place in late June in Manchester's Gay Village, a few months before the Pride weekend. This year's event had live music and comedy. Lauren, a transgender volunteer at the event, told me: "We've got a lot of stigma and hatred against usâ¦ You've got people trying to push us back into the dark and it does make it harder to live our lives."

Another transgender woman I spoke to, who was staying in a hotel in Manchester's Gay Village, said she wanted to be in the city for the event, but was wary of leaving the hotel because she felt unsafe.

Security has also become a central consideration, especially after the events of last month in Berlin, when 21-year-old Abdul Ballout drove a car into a crowd at the city's Pride festival, killing one woman and injuring 29 others. Guy Mathias, from the Security Commonwealth - a trade group for security firms - says he thinks many Pride organisers will review their plans following the Berlin attack.

"Smaller events generally would cost less individually, but they still need many of the same safety measures in place," he adds.

Others think that Pride festivals can create headaches for local residents. Andy Winter, a columnist for the Brighton Argus, attended Pride marches in the 1980s in his role as a Brighton councillor. He recalled in one piece how he was vilified by the press at the time for supporting a pro-LGBT council motion. But last year, he wrote that Brighton's Pride weekend comes with "alcohol and drug-fuelled excesses".

He wrote: "Even though I am not gay, Pride impacts on me. One of the parks I use is 'closed' for ten days... to allow largely straight performers to entertain those able to pay the large entry fee." He added: "The streets are littered with plastics and broken glass. I pity neighbours of the park and surrounding streets who see their driveways and gardens used as toilets."

I've been to dozens of Pride events over the years. Manchester has always been a must. When I was a teenager in Ulverston, Cumbria - a place where I was pretty certain I was the only gay in the village - Manchester always seemed like the bright lights, a land where you could be free and your true self.

This year I'll return again, excited to catch up with my friends and intrigued to see what the new community-focused Pride is all about.

But I suspect there'll be a slightly different mood in the air this year; an awareness that in some parts of the country, Pride has become controversial.

Younger LGBT people still say Pride matters. A 2024 YouGov survey of more than 500 LGBT Britons, aged 16 to 24, found that 90% say it is "very" or "fairly" important that Pride month still exists.

As a young man, I eventually left Ulverston to live in Manchester. But this summer I took a trip back to my old hometown for their Pride festival, a tradition still in its infancy.

The once-familiar cobbled streets looked so different to how I remembered them, lined with cheering locals clapping and filming on phones as a procession bedecked in rainbow flags swept past, led by a brass band playing upbeat gay anthems. It felt a world away from Manchester's famous pop stars and stages covered in corporate logos.

Matt had a similar reflection on returning to Crewe. "What really resonated with me and blew my mind was the fact that it was so family-centred. These small towns put on events that are for the community first and foremost."

As I looked around Ulverston, the national debates that have shaped Pride in recent years felt distant. I was distracted by the small things: people laughing, the spread of ages in attendance. It was the community my teenage self never would have imagined he'd see.

BBC InDepth is the home on the website and app for the best analysis, with fresh perspectives that challenge assumptions and deep reporting on the biggest issues of the day. Emma Barnett and John Simpson bring their pick of the most thought-provoking deep reads and analysis, every Saturday. Sign up for the newsletter here

Are you personally affected by the issues raised in this story?

The once-familiar cobbled streets looked so different to how I remembered them, lined with cheering locals clapping and filming on phones as a procession bedecked in rainbow flags swept past, led by a brass band playing upbeat gay anthems. It felt a world away from Manchester's famous pop stars and stages covered in corporate logos.

Matt had a similar reflection on returning to Crewe. "What really resonated with me and blew my mind was the fact that it was so family-centred. These small towns put on events that are for the community first and foremost."

As I looked around Ulverston, the national debates that have shaped Pride in recent years felt distant. I was distracted by the small things: people laughing, the spread of ages in attendance. It was the community my teenage self never would have imagined he'd see.

articles.title: Demetrius Fleming, 38, Found Hanging In Roanoke Rapids
articles.summary: An ongoing police investigation surrounds the death of a 38-year-old Black man found hanging last Friday morning. The police chief of the city reports that t...
articles.body:
An ongoing police investigation surrounds the death of a 38-year-old Black man found hanging last Friday morning. The police chief of the city reports that the cause of death is yet to be established.

The deceased man has been identified as Demetrius Eugene Fleming. Police Chief Lawrence Wiggins reported that police received a call just a little past 6:45 a.m. about a possible suicide case in the 1900 block of Roanoke Avenue. Fleming was discovered tied with a rope and declared dead at the scene.

According to Wiggins, Fleming was found dead when emergency personnel arrived at the house. Halifax County EMS and the Roanoke Rapids Fire Department were part of the effort. No information has been provided on the type of ligature used.

"We're treating this as an open, equivocal death investigation," Wiggins reported. This means that the cause of death is being investigated without making assumptions about whether it was a suicide, homicide, or accident. Wiggins stated that it would be premature to conclude and that the evidence would determine the cause of death.

At the afternoon press conference, Wiggins said that "anything is on the table" and detectives are exploring all angles of the case. When asked whether another person may be involved, he said everything is under consideration.

An autopsy is being carried out. According to Wiggins, the autopsy will provide the possibility to establish any other injuries on Fleming. Information should be available by Monday; however, it was not available by Tuesday.

According to Wiggins, police are aware of the case's history. He expressed his condolences to the family of Demetrius Fleming and added that they are cooperating with investigators since Friday.

The recent death case follows a similar incident that happened a week ago. Wiggins referred to the Raleigh case, where police ruled the death a suicide, according to WITN.

Chief Rico Boyce of Raleigh Police reported on Aug. 17 that video surveillance footage, along with traffic cameras, showed the 32-year-old man walking alone to the tree carrying an electrical cord, and investigators found no indication of anyone else's involvement. Boyce added that the woman's mother informed investigators of the man's mental problems.

The death of the 32-year-old man became an occasion of fear, pain, and concern for the population, according to the statement made by the North Carolina NAACP and its Raleigh-Apex branch.

The reason why the Raleigh death case received so much attention is the connection of a Black man found hanging from a tree in the South with the history of racist lynchings. Demetrius Eugene Fleming was originally from Roanoke Rapids, was born in January 1988, and his relatives said he was a husband and father.

Persons with information are encouraged to contact Halifax County Crime Stoppers at 252-583-4444 or via the P3 Tips app.
